title: seeds check --against-git: catch mass single-field rewrites
description:
Add `seeds check --against-git`: diff every field of every seed against its value at the previous commit, and flag mass single-field changes.

## Why

This is the detector that catches seeds-wurl in under a second. On 2026-08-31 a bulk agent sweep replaced 83 of 306 titles with a scratchpad path in a single commit. The diff was 174 lines of JSONL and nobody reads that. **A mass single-field change across most of the corpus is trivially detectable and was not detected** — it survived three days and three subsequent commits.

The shape to flag is exactly that: one field, changed across a large fraction of the corpus, in one commit.

## It is also the right hook gate

A commit rewriting 87 files has no cheap human review. Demanding explicit confirmation for that shape **subsumes gating `D` and `R`** in `git diff --name-status`, which the deliberation had wanted separately so that `rm <seed-file>` does not become the de facto delete verb (there is no `delete` verb, and @aguynamedryan is content with that).

## Scope note

Detection at commit is not immutability. An agent can read corrupt state at any point before the commit fires. That is not closable and is accepted — it bounds damage to one working session rather than five weeks.

Source: seeds-wurl, seeds-sdhc.2, seeds-ebg1
acceptance_criteria: 'seeds check --against-git' compares every field against its value at the previous commit and flags a single field changed across a large fraction of the corpus in one commit; a test reproduces the seeds-wurl shape (83 of 306 titles replaced with a path in one commit) and the check flags it.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-31 on branch seeds-4co.4/check-smells-and-git.

Design picks made under the overnight ambiguity ruling (code-only, 2-way):

1. WHICH TWO STATES. 'the previous commit' is read as the pre-commit gate
   reads it: the working store is compared against HEAD. When the store is
   byte-identical to HEAD there is nothing uncommitted to gate, so it falls
   back to HEAD~1 vs HEAD and audits the commit that just landed -- seeds-wurl
   needed exactly that second reading, since the sweep was committed and then
   survived three days. The output always names both revisions ('308 seed(s)
   at HEAD~1, compared with HEAD'), because 'no findings' only reassures once
   you know what was compared.
2. THRESHOLDS. A field must differ on >=20% of the before-corpus AND on >=10
   seeds. 83/306 = 27.1% clears it with margin; retyping a dozen seeds in a
   300-seed store is 3.9% and does not.
3. DELETIONS. A seed present before and absent after counts as changing EVERY
   field. That is what makes the rule subsume gating D and R in 'git diff
   --name-status' with no second rule: there is no delete verb, and 'rm' over
   40 of 100 seeds trips all 12 fields at once. A single deletion is 1% and is
   not flagged.
4. IT GATES. --against-git findings DO set the exit code (unlike --smells).
   No git at all is a loud error, not a quiet skip -- a comparison the operator
   asked for that silently could not run is the green-while-broken shape. An
   unborn HEAD is NOT that case: it is a real, empty before-state, corpus 0,
   no findings.
5. FALSE-POSITIVE GUARD. tags and relationships are compared
   order-insensitively; a reordered block sequence is a no-op and must never
   demand a human decision on a commit.

Verified at real size: 306 seeds committed, 83 titles replaced with
/tmp/claude-scratch/notes.md, committed -> exactly one finding, 'title differs
on 83 of 306 seeds (27% of the corpus, 83 rewritten) between HEAD~1 and HEAD'.
Also reproduced against the real 308-seed corpus rendered into a temp git repo.
An ordinary single-seed edit (1 of 306) is not flagged, in either direction.
close_reason: check --against-git flags a single field rewritten across >=20% and >=10 seeds between two revisions; reproduces the 83-of-306 wurl shape as exactly one finding naming only title; a deleted seed counts as changing every field, which subsumes gating D/R

title: seeds check --smells: the reporting tier that does not fail
description:
Add the second tier to `seeds check`: smells. These REPORT and never fail — `check --smells`, and excluded from the exit code.

## Why a separate tier

Some things worth noticing cannot support being a gate. Supersession discipline is the clear case: a long body with many commits of history and no `[!SUPERSEDED]` marker is a *candidate* for attention, never an error. Naming the tier keeps discipline-shaped checks from being promoted into gates they cannot carry.

## Smells to implement

- a long body with many commits of history and no supersession marker
- a body byte-identical to another seed's

## This tier IS `tend`

`tend` was designed as a review-and-rule pass that would compress at tend time. seeds-sdhc rejected the compression (*"tending never destroys"*), and once supersession is marked at write time by the agent that learned it (seeds-sdhc.3), nothing editorial is left for `tend` to do — only *noticing*, which is this.

@aguynamedryan, ruled 2026-08-31: *"let's remove suggest/tend for now ... tend never really got used and the one time I tried to use it, I was told it wasn't the right time."*

So **do not build a `tend` verb.** It was never built in the first place (verified — it is not a CLI command), and it should not be. This bead is where its surviving function lives.

Source: seeds-sdhc.2, seeds-sdhc.3
acceptance_criteria: 'seeds check --smells' reports a long body with many commits and no supersession marker, and a body byte-identical to another seed's; smells never affect the exit code; no 'tend' verb is added.
notes:
Gains one smell from seeds-4co.3 by ruling (@aguynamedryan, 2026-08-31): an empty body. Expect ~31 standing entries on this repo, most of them legitimately-open question-type seeds. Its first real use is already proven: it surfaces six test fixtures left in the design database (seeds-71 and its nesting-demo descendants, seeds-136) that nobody noticed for 205+ days. See seeds-tz66.
ACCEPTANCE-CRITERIA GAP (recorded 2026-08-31): this bead's acceptance criteria list two smells — a long body with no supersession marker, and a body byte-identical to another seed's — but NOT the empty body, which @aguynamedryan moved here from seeds-4co.3's violations tier. The ruling is in the notes; the acceptance field was never updated. Implement all three.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-31 on branch seeds-4co.4/check-smells-and-git.

Design picks made under the overnight ambiguity ruling (code-only, 2-way):

1. --smells is ADDITIVE, not a mode. 'seeds check --smells' still runs the
   violations tier and still exits non-zero on a violation; the smells section
   is printed after it under a '⚠' marker (violations keep '✗') and never
   touches the exit code. A hook can therefore run 'seeds check --smells
   --against-git' and get all three tiers in one pass.
2. The long-body smell needs commit counts, so git plumbing landed in a NEW
   module src/seeds/githistory.py rather than inside gitstage.py, which stays
   scoped to 'what is staged right now'. Outside a git repo the smell is
   SILENT rather than degrading to body length alone -- length alone selects a
   third of the corpus, which is exactly what the AND exists to avoid.
3. Thresholds measured off the real corpus, not guessed: LONG_BODY_BYTES=2000
   (median body 1197, p75 2621; 2000 selects 104 of 308) AND MANY_COMMITS=5.

All three ruled smells implemented: empty-body, unsuperseded-long-body,
duplicate-body. No tend verb added; TestThereIsNoTendVerb pins that.

Measured against the real 314-seed corpus rendered read-only into a temp dir
(308 records after the 6 ruled fixtures drop): 32 smells, exit 0 -- 25
empty-body and 7 duplicate-body (three groups of old 'Abandoned: consolidated
into ...' stubs). unsuperseded-long-body contributed 0 there because the store
is not converted yet and so has no seed-file git history to count.

NOTE / out of scope: the ruling quoted was 'remove suggest/tend'. 'tend' never
existed. 'suggest' DOES exist (cli.py:727, similarity search over seeds) and
was left alone -- retiring it is not in either bead's acceptance criteria and
should be filed separately if wanted.
close_reason: check --smells is additive: empty-body, unsuperseded-long-body (2000 bytes AND 5+ commits, thresholds measured off the corpus), duplicate-body; smells print under a warning marker and never touch the exit code; no tend verb, pinned by a test

title: changelog_coverage gates the generator, not the artifact — a stale hand-written CHANGELOG section passes it
description:
scripts/changelog_coverage.py verifies that every commit in a range either renders in git-cliff's output or matches a deliberate skip rule in cliff.toml. That gates the GENERATOR. It says nothing about whether the hand-polished section actually in CHANGELOG.md kept up with it.

The gap is not theoretical — it bit twice during the 0.6.0 release. The section was written, then more work landed, and the committed CHANGELOG.md silently fell behind the generated notes. Both times it was caught by diffing generated-vs-CHANGELOG by hand:

    just changelog-release vX.Y.Z | grep -oE '/commit/[0-9a-f]{7}'  |  sort -u
    sed -n '/^## \[X.Y.Z\]/,/^## \[/p' CHANGELOG.md | grep -oE '/commit/[0-9a-f]{7}' | sort -u
    comm -23 <(generated) <(committed)

That check currently exists only as a habit, not as code. changelog_coverage.py exits 0 on a range whose CHANGELOG section is months out of date.

Note the root cause of both incidents was PROCESS, not tooling: CONTRIBUTING's checklist puts the changelog at step 2, immediately before the commit and tag at steps 3-4, and it was instead written early and then invalidated by further work. Writing it last removes both failures for free. This bead is the belt to that suspenders — worth having because the ordering mistake is easy to make and invisible when made.
design:
Extend scripts/changelog_coverage.py with a second assertion, or add a sibling mode, that compares the generated entries for a version against the section already in CHANGELOG.md:

- MISSING-FROM-CHANGELOG: generated, absent from the committed section.
- PHANTOM: referenced in the committed section, not in the range (catches stale entries after a rebase or a botched merge).

The hard part is that the polished section DELIBERATELY omits entries — 13 in 0.6.0: dependabot bumps, chore bookkeeping, CI internals, a commit superseded inside the same release, and the commit that wrote the section itself. A naive 'everything generated must appear' check would fail every release and get ignored, which is worse than no check.

So the omissions need to be machine-readable. Options, unexamined:
- A skip list in cliff.toml one level up — a [changelog.omit] table listing hashes with a one-line reason each.
- A marker comment inside the CHANGELOG section itself (e.g. an HTML comment listing intentionally-omitted hashes), keeping the record next to the artifact.
- Loosen the rule: only assert that every commit git-cliff puts under Added / Fixed / Changed / Breaking appears, and let Documentation and Tooling be freely pruned.

The third is cheapest and probably catches everything that matters — the two real misses were a feat and a fix.

Whichever is chosen, the reason for an omission must be recorded, or the check degrades into a hash allowlist nobody can audit.
acceptance_criteria: A release whose CHANGELOG.md section is missing a generated feat/fix/breaking entry fails the check and names the entry. A section referencing a commit outside the range fails and names it. The 0.6.0 section as shipped PASSES, with its 13 deliberate omissions accounted for by whatever mechanism is chosen rather than by loosening the check until it says nothing. CONTRIBUTING's checklist calls it. Tests use hand-built inputs with hand-computed verdicts, including one case that must pass and one that must fail.
close_reason: changelog_coverage grows --section: gates the committed CHANGELOG artifact with a category rule plus a reason-carrying per-commit omission marker; CONTRIBUTING calls it as release step 3

title: Release step 7 and CLAUDE.md's deploy section both name a path that is shadowed on this host
description:
Two documented ways to refresh the global 'seeds' CLI after a release, and on titan neither one does anything to the binary that actually runs.

CONTRIBUTING.md step 7:
    uv cache clean seeds && uv tool install --reinstall .
CLAUDE.md 'Deploy to Global CLI':
    uv cache clean seeds && uv tool uninstall seeds && uv tool install --reinstall .

Measured on titan 2026-08-31:
- 'which -a seeds' resolves to /home/ryan/.nix-profile/bin/seeds, a symlink into /nix/store/...-seeds-0.5.0/bin/seeds.
- 'uv tool list' does NOT list seeds. It has never been installed that way here.
- PATH order puts /home/ryan/.nix-profile/bin at position 6 and /home/ryan/.local/bin (where uv tool installs) at position 7. So even if the documented command ran, the uv-installed binary would be SHADOWED by the nix one.

The real deploy path on this host is nix: ~/.config/home-manager/flake.nix takes 'github:outcomesinsights/seeds' as an input and applies seeds.overlays.default; modules/packages.nix says in as many words 'Bump it with nix flake update seeds, not by editing anything here.' That path requires the release TAG TO BE PUSHED first, which the uv-based instructions do not.

Consequence: a maintainer finishing a release, running step 7, and then checking 'seeds --version' sees the OLD version and has no idea why. Right now this repo is at 0.6.0 while 'seeds --version' reports 0.5.0.

Secondary, already established while investigating: the two documented commands also disagree with each other about whether an explicit 'uv tool uninstall' is needed. It is not — 'uv tool install --reinstall' is documented as 'Reinstall all packages, regardless of whether they're already installed. Implies --refresh'. CONTRIBUTING is right and CLAUDE.md's extra uninstall is redundant. That disagreement was flagged by the agent that fixed seeds-76q and left unresolved; it is resolved here.
design:
Do not simply pick one of the two commands — both describe a deploy path that is not the one in use on this host.

The instruction should distinguish the install method rather than assume one:
- If seeds is on the nix profile (the case on titan): the refresh is 'nix flake update seeds' in ~/.config/home-manager followed by a switch, and it requires the tag to be pushed first. Say so, and say it comes AFTER step 5 (push) rather than being an independent step.
- If seeds was installed with 'uv tool': 'uv cache clean seeds && uv tool install --reinstall .' is correct and the explicit uninstall is redundant.

A one-line 'which seeds' check tells the maintainer which case they are in; leading with that is cheaper than describing both and hoping the reader picks right.

Fix both CONTRIBUTING.md step 7 and CLAUDE.md's 'Deploy to Global CLI' section, since they carry the same wrong instruction and drifting them apart again is the failure mode.
acceptance_criteria: CONTRIBUTING.md step 7 and CLAUDE.md's deploy section agree with each other and with how seeds is actually installed. Both name the 'which seeds' check that disambiguates. The nix path states its dependency on the tag being pushed. Neither instructs a redundant 'uv tool uninstall'. Verified by following whichever branch applies on this host and confirming 'seeds --version' actually changes.
notes:
VERIFIED FACTS for the fix (parent, 2026-08-31) — do not re-derive:

The nix path, read from ~/.config/home-manager:
- flake.nix declares input 'seeds = { url = "github:outcomesinsights/seeds"; inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs"; }' and applies 'overlays = [ seeds.overlays.default ]'.
- IMPORTANT: the input has NO ref/tag pin, so it tracks the DEFAULT BRANCH (main). The refresh therefore needs 'git push origin main' to have landed — pushing the tag alone is not enough, and the instruction should say main rather than the tag.
- modules/packages.nix installs pkgs.seeds and says verbatim: 'Bump it with , not by editing anything here.'
- So the sequence is: push main -> 'nix flake update seeds' in ~/.config/home-manager -> switch.

home-manager ALREADY documents the shadowing that this bead is about, in modules/packages.nix:
  'Installing it puts seeds on the nix profile PATH on all hosts, superseding any leftover uv tool install copy at ~/.local/bin/seeds. Per-host post-switch cleanup: uv tool uninstall seeds (run AFTER just switch so nix copy is already in place).'
The seeds repo's own docs simply never got that memo. Worth noting in the fix that the two repos disagreed, so the next reader knows which is authoritative.

On the uninstall disagreement flagged during seeds-76q: 'uv tool install --reinstall' is documented as 'Reinstall all packages, regardless of whether they are already installed. Implies --refresh', so an explicit uninstall is redundant FOR A REINSTALL. But note home-manager uses 'uv tool uninstall seeds' for a different purpose — one-time cleanup of a stale ~/.local/bin copy after moving to nix. CLAUDE.md conflates the two. The fix should keep those purposes distinct rather than just deleting the uninstall.

Measured on titan: 'which -a seeds' -> /home/ryan/.nix-profile/bin/seeds only; 'uv tool list' does not contain seeds; PATH has ~/.nix-profile/bin at position 6 and ~/.local/bin at position 7.
close_reason: Both docs lead with 'which seeds' and branch: nix flake update (needs main pushed) vs uv tool reinstall; shadowing explained in both

title: seeds update: accept content from a file or stdin
description:
Add --content-file <path> and --content - (stdin) to 'seeds update', so a body can be supplied without passing it through argv.

Today --content is only -c TEXT. On this project's own corpus (302 seeds: median body 1.0KB, p90 4.6KB, max 15.0KB, 5 bodies over 10KB) that means an agent folding a divergence reads the whole body into context and re-emits it verbatim in a shell argument — roughly twice the body in tokens, with truncation or a mangled quote silently corrupting deliberation.

This is a general gap, not only a divergence problem, which is why it was chosen over the purpose-built 'seeds absorb' fold: it survives the 0.7 storage change, and the divergence failure mode it currently serves does not.
acceptance_criteria: 'seeds update <id> --content-file <path>' replaces the body from the file. 'seeds update <id> --content -' reads the body from stdin. Both respect the existing edited-seed guard that refuses a wholesale --content replacement (--replace still required to override). --content-file, --content - and -c TEXT are mutually exclusive and a combination is refused rather than resolved by precedence. Tests cover each input path plus the mutual exclusion.
notes: Spelling picked (deliberate): stdin is the sentinel `-` on the EXISTING -c/--content option, exactly as the bead preferred. Click handles it fine — no third option name was needed, so the `--content-file -` fallback was not taken. `--content-file -` is instead REFUSED with a message pointing at `--content -`, so stdin keeps one spelling rather than two. Second pick: a single trailing newline is stripped from file/stdin input (rstrip("\n")), because editors and `>` redirects always add one and `-c TEXT` never carries one — without it the same body would differ by delivery route. Mutual exclusion is between --content and --content-file (the -c TEXT vs --content - case is one option, so Click already makes it unrepeatable); combining them exits 1 with an "ambiguous" refusal rather than a precedence rule, matching _reject_ambiguous_tag_flags.
close_reason: seeds update accepts --content-file PATH and --content - (stdin); guard and mutual exclusion enforced

title: Divergence remediation makes the operator paste a whole seed body through argv
description:
When `seeds sync` refuses on a `content` divergence, the recovery it prints is:

    # compare, then rebuild the body with the on-disk text first
    seeds show <id>
    seeds update <id> --replace -c '<on-disk text><newer text>'

That asks the operator to reconstruct the entire body by hand and pass it through argv. `seeds update` has no file or stdin input for `--content` -- only `-c TEXT` -- so there is no cheaper route available even to someone who wants one.

## Cost, measured on this project's own database

302 seeds: median body 1.0KB, p90 4.6KB, max 15.0KB. 35 bodies over 4KB, 5 over 10KB.

For an agent -- which is who actually runs this -- the whole body has to be read into context and re-emitted verbatim in a shell argument, twice the body in tokens for a single fold, with truncation or a mangled quote silently corrupting deliberation. The seeds most likely to diverge are the long, actively-edited ones, so the cost is concentrated exactly where the operation is most common.

## The deeper point

seeds already HAS both texts -- `find_divergence` computed the comparison to raise the error in the first place (it carries `on_disk` and `in_db` on each Divergence). Asking a human to retype the concatenation is asking them to redo arithmetic the tool has already done and is holding in memory.

## Options, unexamined

- `seeds update <id> --content-file <path>` / `--content -` for stdin. Smallest change; fixes the argv cost but still makes the operator assemble the text.
- A purpose-built fold, e.g. `seeds absorb <id>` or `seeds sync --absorb`, that takes the on-disk body and folds it in itself. Removes the assembly step entirely; the tool has both halves.
- Leave the message but stop implying a one-liner: say plainly that the body must be rebuilt and point at an editor.

Reported by an adversarial review in a parallel session (seeds-7f) alongside two defects fixed in 55bf114; this one is a UX cost rather than a defect, hence separate.

Note for whoever picks this up: if the storage question under deliberation in seeds-lcfa / seeds-fkb8 moves to per-seed files with a mutable body, the content-divergence failure mode disappears and this remediation goes with it. Check that before building the larger option.
design:
RULED (Ryan, 2026-08-28): option 1 — fix the message AND add a non-argv content input. NOT the purpose-built fold.

Two parts:
1. Add --content-file <path> and --content - (stdin) to 'seeds update'. This closes a general gap that exists independent of divergence: there is no file or stdin route for --content today, only -c TEXT.
2. Fix the divergence remediation message to stop implying a one-liner, and point at the new input.

Why not 'seeds absorb': the content-divergence failure mode disappears entirely in 0.7, when the wholesale rewrite of a single JSONL goes away. A purpose-built fold would be machinery for a problem with one release left to live. The stdin/file input survives the storage change because it is about how content reaches the CLI, not about the store.
acceptance_criteria:
- Folding an on-disk body into the database no longer requires passing the body through argv.
- The path taken works on a 15KB body without truncation.
- The divergence message names the cheaper route rather than the argv one-liner.
- Regression test covers the fold on a body larger than 10KB.
- `uv run pytest` exits 0 and `uv run ruff check` is clean.
close_reason: Divergence refusal now points at --content-file/--content - instead of asking for a whole body through argv

title: A .seeds dir with no DB sends users to 'seeds init', which then refuses
description:
When `.seeds/` exists but `seeds.db` does not, every command names the wrong recovery and `seeds init` contradicts them.

Measured (a project whose DB was deleted, JSONL intact):

    $ seeds list     -> Error: seeds not initialized. Run 'seeds init' first.
    $ seeds sync     -> Error: seeds not initialized. Run 'seeds init' first.
    $ seeds doctor   -> Error: seeds not initialized. Run 'seeds init' first.
    $ seeds init     -> seeds already initialized in .../.seeds

A closed loop: three commands send you to `init`, and `init` refuses without creating the database.

## It is recoverable, and that is the point

`seeds import` fixes it instantly — it uses the bootstrap seam, creating the schema and recovering the prefix from the JSONL:

    $ seeds import
    Imported: 1 created, 0 updated, 0 skipped

Nothing in any of those four messages mentions it.

## Why this matters more than it looks

`.seeds/seeds.db` is gitignored (`.seeds/.gitignore` excludes `*.db`), and only `seeds.jsonl` is tracked. **So this is exactly the state of every fresh clone.** A new user clones a seeds-using repo, runs `seeds list`, is told to run `seeds init`, and is then told the project is already initialized. `seeds import` is the documented fresh-clone rehydration path and the CLI never names it.

This is the same class of defect as seeds-1x6b: the tool confidently says something wrong at the moment the user most needs it to be right.

## Shape

Make the "not initialized" error distinguish the two states. When `.seeds/` exists and holds a `seeds.jsonl` but no DB, say so and name `seeds import`. Consider having `seeds init` in that state either bootstrap from the JSONL itself or point at `seeds import` rather than reporting "already initialized", which is true of the directory and false of the thing the user needs.

Found while verifying bead seeds-jlt.
acceptance_criteria:
- With `.seeds/` present, a JSONL present, and no seeds.db: `seeds list` names `seeds import` in its error rather than `seeds init`.
- `seeds init` in that state does not report a bare "already initialized" — it either rehydrates or names `seeds import`.
- A genuinely uninitialized directory (no `.seeds/` at all) still says "Run 'seeds init' first".
- Regression test covers both states.
- `uv run pytest` exits 0 and `uv run ruff check` is clean.
close_reason: The 'not initialized' error now distinguishes three states via _uninitialized_error(): no .seeds at all still says 'seeds init'; .seeds with a JSONL but no DB names 'seeds import' and explains why (DB gitignored, JSONL tracked); an empty .seeds initializes normally instead of refusing. seeds init no longer reports 'already initialized' over a directory holding no database. Verified all three states by hand plus a test that actually runs the advice and confirms recovery. 710 pass, ruff clean.

title: seeds search crashes on any hyphenated query (raw FTS5 MATCH)
description:
`seeds search` passes the user's query straight into an FTS5 `MATCH` (src/seeds/db.py:1242, `WHERE seeds_fts MATCH ?` with `params = [query]`). FTS5 treats `-` as a syntax character, so any hyphenated term is parsed as a column filter and the query dies with an uncaught sqlite3.OperationalError plus a full traceback.

Observed on seeds 0.5.0:

    $ seeds search "seeds-to-beads"
    sqlite3.OperationalError: no such column: to

Reproduces for every hyphenated query tried -- `seeds-to-beads`, `pre-commit`, `foo-bar` -- while a bare word (`beads`) works. This is not an edge case in this repo: hyphenated tags and skill names (`seeds-to-beads`, `resolve-seeds-from-beads`, `pre-commit`) are exactly what someone searches for, and seed IDs are hyphenated too.

Found while searching for prior deliberation on the seeds-to-beads skill (seeds-w42l).

## Likely fix

Quote the query for FTS5 before it reaches MATCH -- wrap in double quotes with internal `"` doubled, or tokenize and quote each term -- so hyphens and other FTS5 operators are literal. Decide deliberately whether any FTS5 operator syntax stays reachable by users; if not, quote everything.

Whatever the fix, a raw sqlite3 traceback should not be the user-facing failure mode.
acceptance_criteria:
- `seeds search "seeds-to-beads"` exits 0 and returns the seeds whose text contains that term.
- `seeds search "pre-commit"` exits 0.
- Regression test covers a hyphenated query and asserts no exception.
- A query containing a double quote does not crash.
- `uv run pytest` exits 0.
close_reason: Fixed: sanitize_fts_query (src/seeds/models.py) quotes terms FTS5 would parse as syntax, so a hyphenated query searches instead of raising. Wired into db.search and db.suggest. Documented operator syntax (phrases, prefix*, uppercase AND/OR/NOT, NEAR) survives untouched; anything else is treated as literal text. Also fixed a silent variant: suggest tokenizes keeping hyphens and swallowed the OperationalError, so ANY hyphenated dedup query returned 'no matches' rather than crashing -- verified against the pre-fix 0.5.0 binary. 18 regression tests added; 687 pass, ruff clean.

title: seeds-to-beads: consult the user on unsettled decisions by default, --autonomous to opt out
description:
Change the default behavior of the `seeds-to-beads` skill (src/seeds/plugin/claude-plugin/skills/seeds-to-beads/SKILL.md) so it stops and asks the user about decisions the deliberation left open BEFORE writing the bead that depends on them. Add `--autonomous` to restore the prior one-pass behavior.

Source: seeds-w42l (extends seeds-152.4, seeds-186; feeds seeds-184)

## Motivation

The skill converted in one pass: it made every call the deliberation had left open, silently, and handed the result to an executing agent that could not ask either. The guess is invisible by the time it costs anything -- it reads to the executor as a settled decision.

## Locked decisions (do not re-open)

- Consulting is the DEFAULT; one-pass is opt-in via `--autonomous`. Ryan verbatim: "as beads are being generated, if the process surfaces decisions to be made that would benefit from user input, the skill should prompt the user before making the bead so the bead has complete input from the user" / "I'd like to add a flag for 'autonomous' where the current behavior of just plunging on ahead seems to be the norm".
- Ask BEFORE the bead is written, not after -- a question costs a sentence, a baked-in guess costs a round of rework.
- The bar for asking is bounded, because an interrogation would be worse than plunging ahead. Ask only for: scope boundary; taste/UX/naming on a human-readable surface; something the seeds raised and never landed; acceptance criteria needing a definition picked before they can be mechanical; sequencing that encodes a design commitment.
- Explicitly do NOT ask about anything the deliberation already settled (re-opening a locked decision is the failure this skill exists to prevent), mechanical decomposition/wording, or anything answerable by reading the repo.
- Batch questions after a full analysis pass; offer options with a recommendation.
- `--autonomous` is not silent: each call it would otherwise have asked about is recorded in the bead as `Assumed: ... -- the deliberation didn't settle this` and gathered into the closing summary.
- Answers that settle something the originating seed had open get carried back to the seed (`seeds answer` / a note), so the deliberation record is not poorer than the beads it produced.
acceptance_criteria:
- SKILL.md frontmatter description mentions both the consult default and `--autonomous`.
- SKILL.md contains a consult-before-you-create section listing what to ask about AND what not to ask about.
- SKILL.md contains an `--autonomous` section stating it records skipped calls as explicit assumptions.
- README.md's `seeds:seeds-to-beads` bullet describes the consult default and the flag.
- `uv run pytest` exits 0.
close_reason: Implemented in SKILL.md + README. All five acceptance criteria verified (grep checks pass; pytest 668 passed). Process note: the edit was made BEFORE this bead or seeds-w42l existed -- I went straight from Ryan's request to implementation, skipping deliberate->beads->implement. The seed and bead were written afterward to record the decision, not to authorize it. The diff was already correct so it was not reverted and re-done.

title: Enforce the git test sandbox as the single door, and close HOME-based config paths
description:
Follow-on hardening to seeds-p0x (3919c00). The containment works; two gaps remain. Deliberation: seed seeds-ngez.1.

GAP 1 - the single door is a convention, not an invariant. tests/githelpers.py is currently the only path to real git, but nothing enforces it. Two previous agents independently wrote their own copy of _git/_git_init, and that duplication is exactly how one copy came to poison the real repo. Nothing stops a third copy appearing in the next bead.

GAP 2 - HOME is still readable. git_env() redirects GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM to os.devnull, which covers ~/.gitconfig, but git still consults HOME for include.path chains, init.templateDir and credential helpers. Measured on titan 2026-08-26: neither is set globally here, so this is theoretical today. Two lines closes the category rather than the instance.

Explicitly NOT in scope, and decided rather than deferred: replacing the real-git tests with mocks. A mock encodes what we predict git does, and every bug in this family was git doing something we did not predict (GIT_DIR overriding cwd, core.bare making git init re-initialize a real repo as bare, GIT_AUTHOR_* outranking config). A mocked suite would have been green through all three; the third was caught only because a real commit ran. The mock/real split already exists in test_gitstage.py and the line is in the right place.
design:
1. Enforcement test scanning tests/*.py. It must detect actual INVOCATION - subprocess.run/Popen/check_output with a git argv - not the string "git", because the legitimate mocked tests in test_gitstage.py mention ["git", "diff"] inside a patched subprocess.run and must not trip it. tests/githelpers.py is the sole allowed file. Prefer an AST walk over a regex so the check cannot be fooled by formatting.

2. Add HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME to git_env(), pointed at a directory inside the sandbox.

Rejected for gap 1: a ruff lint rule. It cannot express "except in this one file" cleanly enough to be worth the configuration.
acceptance_criteria:
- A test fails if any file in tests/ other than githelpers.py invokes real git, and it does NOT trip on the existing mocked-subprocess tests in test_gitstage.py.
- The enforcement test is itself verified against a hand-built offending sample, so it is known to fail when it should.
- git_env() redirects HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME into the sandbox, with a test asserting it.
- Full suite green, mypy strict and ruff clean, and the suite still passes when run as this repo's own pre-commit pytest hook.
close_reason: Implemented in 1cde6d2. tests/test_git_single_door.py walks the AST of every file in tests/ and fails if any but githelpers.py invokes git via subprocess; nine tests exercise the detector itself on hand-built samples both directions, including the three mention-only patterns (CompletedProcess literal, argv comparison, patch()) that must not trip it. It found a real bypass on first run (test_host_global_config_is_not_readable called subprocess.run directly), now routed through git() and made non-vacuous with a skip. git_env() also redirects HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME into the sandbox, closing include.path/templateDir/credential-helper paths that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL does not cover. 668 passed, mypy strict and ruff clean, suite green under the pre-commit hook.

title: Parameterize _guard_content_replacement: it prints 'seeds update --content' advice to 'seeds answer' callers
description:
Source: seeds-3dkj (a SEED — `seeds show seeds-3dkj`). Discovered by the implementing agent while shipping seeds-btr on 2026-08-26, reported on both receipts as a related defect, verified afterwards.

## The defect

`_guard_content_replacement` (src/seeds/cli.py:121-161) hardcodes remediation prose for the `update` command:

    Error: <id> has been edited since it was created -- --content would discard N characters of deliberation.
      Would discard: <first line>
      Add to it instead:      seeds update <id> --append "..."
      Discard it on purpose:  seeds update <id> --content "..." --replace

It now has two callers — cli.py:1004 (`update`) and cli.py:1133 (`answer`). A user who trips the guard via `seeds answer` is told about a `--content` flag that `answer` does not have, and pointed at `seeds update` rather than at `seeds answer <id> "..." --append` / `--replace`, which is what they want and what now exists.

This is the SAME defect class as seeds-pfe: guidance that does not match the command it is advising about.

## LOCKED DECISION (Ryan, 2026-08-26)

Option (a) from the seed: parameterize the helper so one guard renders correct advice per caller. Rejected: stripping the prose generic (loses the copy-pasteable one-liner) and returning a decision for each caller to print its own (duplication is the drift risk parameterizing avoids).

## Constraint that carries the lesson

The per-caller prose must be REQUIRED, with no default. The defect being fixed is a second caller silently inheriting the first caller's prose; a default parameter set to update's wording would reintroduce exactly that, and the next caller would ship the same bug again. Make it impossible to add a caller without stating its own remediation.

## Message shapes

`update`:  "<id> has been edited since it was created -- --content would discard N characters..."
           append:  seeds update <id> --append "..."
           replace: seeds update <id> --content "..." --replace

`answer`:  "<id> has already been answered -- answering again would discard N characters..."
           append:  seeds answer <id> "..." --append
           replace: seeds answer <id> "..." --replace

Common to both and unchanged: the "Would discard: <first line>" line and the closing note that --replace does not erase anything because the old body survives in git history.

## Acceptance criteria

- `uv run pytest` exits 0, at or above the current 579.
- A test asserts the `update` guard prints `seeds update` remediation naming --content/--append/--replace.
- A test asserts the `answer` guard prints `seeds answer` remediation, and asserts the string "--content" does NOT appear in its output. That negative assertion is the regression this bead exists to pin.
- `grep -n "_guard_content_replacement" src/seeds/cli.py` shows both call sites passing their own prose.
- `uv run mypy src/`, `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .` all exit 0.
close_reason: Guard remediation is now per-caller via a required GuardCopy (no defaults); answer's refusal names seeds answer and never --content

title: pre-push does not actually match CI: missing the Python matrix and the entire nix job
description:
The CI-gates policy's mental contract is "if pre-push passes, CI passes." It does not hold today.

CI runs three jobs; pre-push runs part of one:

| CI job | steps | in pre-push? |
|---|---|---|
| lint | ruff check, ruff format --check, mypy src/ | YES |
| test | pytest on **3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13** | only the local interpreter (3.13) |
| nix | `flake check --all-systems --no-build`, `flake check`, `nix run . -- --version` | **NO** |

So 3.10/3.11/3.12 and the whole nix path are unverified until CI runs — which for a private repo is billed minutes spent discovering what a local check could have caught.

## Cost is measured, not guessed

Timed on titan against the current tree:

```
current pre-push pytest (3.13 only)      9s
+ matrix 3.10, 3.11, 3.12               +29s
+ nix flake check --all-systems --no-build  +4s  (warm)
+ nix flake check                        +3s  (warm)
                                        ------
added                                    ~36s
```

The policy note in CLAUDE.md says pre-push is "rare enough that ~30-60s of wait is acceptable." Adding 36s lands within that. Full parity is affordable — this was worth measuring, since the assumption going in was 2-4 minutes, which would NOT have been.

Caveat to keep honest: the nix timings are warm-cache. The first run after a `flake.lock` change will be substantially slower.

## Work

Add to the `pre-push` stage in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, alongside the existing hooks:

1. **pytest across 3.10-3.12.** 3.13 is already covered by the existing `pytest (full suite)` hook via the local interpreter — do not run it twice. Use `uv run --python <v> --no-sync pytest`.
2. **The three nix commands**, matching `.github/workflows/ci.yml` exactly.

**The nix hooks MUST skip gracefully when `nix` is not on PATH.** This repo is public; a contributor without nix must not be blocked from pushing. Guard with `command -v nix` and exit 0 with a short notice when absent. Do NOT make nix a hard requirement.

Do not bake `--extra-experimental-features` into the hook if the local nix already has flakes enabled; match what CI does and let it fail loudly if the local install is misconfigured — but verify which applies on this box before deciding.

## Then make the claim true

Once the gate matches, say so where the contract lives. If a gap is deliberately left (e.g. the coverage flag), state it explicitly rather than leaving "matches CI" as an unqualified claim that quietly is not.
acceptance_criteria:
- `.pre-commit-config.yaml` has pre-push hooks covering pytest on 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12 (3.13 already covered), plus all three nix commands from ci.yml.
- `uv run pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files` passes and visibly runs the new hooks.
- Every CI step has a pre-push counterpart: diff `yq '.jobs[].steps[].run' .github/workflows/ci.yml` against the pre-push entries and confirm nothing is missing except deliberate, documented exceptions.
- With `nix` unavailable, the nix hooks SKIP rather than fail: verify by running the hook's command with PATH stripped of nix (e.g. `env PATH=/usr/bin:/bin <hook command>`) and confirming exit 0.
- A real push still works end-to-end (`git push` on a no-op commit, or `--dry-run`).
- Total added pre-push wall time is measured and recorded in the bead notes.
close_reason: pre-push now covers all three CI jobs: lint, pytest on 3.10-3.13, and the nix job. Nix hook skips with exit 0 when nix is absent (verified with PATH stripped). Full stage measured at 79s. Only deliberate gap is --cov, which gates nothing.

title: Flaky test: test_real_hash_seed_ref_accepted asserts a property of a randomly generated ID
description:
`tests/test_cli.py::TestBase36RefValidation::test_real_hash_seed_ref_accepted` fails intermittently — roughly 1 run in 33. Caught while merging seeds-agk.2 (a full-suite run came back `1 failed, 570 passed`, then passed on the next five).

Landed with seeds-819. Not caused by seeds-agk.2.

## Cause

Line ~1634:

```python
first = cli_runner.invoke(main, ["jot", "First seed"])
first_id = _extract_jot_id(first.output)
assert not first_id.split("-", 1)[1].isdigit(), first_id
```

The test needs a *hash-shaped* ID to exercise the base36 path, so it asserts the freshly minted ID is not all-digits. But base36 is `[0-9a-z]`, so an all-digit suffix like `seeds-060` is a perfectly ordinary hash. Measured on the real generator:

```
all-digit 3-char hashes: 593/20000 = 2.96%   (expected (10/36)^3 = 2.14%)
```

So ~3% of runs mint an all-digit ID and the assertion blows up. The test is asserting a property of a random value rather than controlling it.

This is the **same underlying fact** that caused seeds-skc (`rename_prefix` treating all-digit hashes as sequential IDs). Worth checking whether any other test makes the same assumption while you are in there.

## Fix direction (pick one deliberately)

- **Control the ID instead of asserting about it.** Construct the seed directly with a known hash-shaped ID (e.g. `Database.create_seed(Seed(id="seeds-k3n7", ...))`, as other tests in the file already do) rather than minting one via `jot` and hoping. This is the obvious fix — the test's subject should not be random.
- Or seed/patch the generator so the minted ID is deterministic for this test.

Do NOT simply loop until a non-digit ID appears, and do NOT delete the assertion — the test genuinely needs a hash-shaped ID, and silently accepting an all-digit one would make it pass while testing the numeric path instead.
acceptance_criteria:
- `tests/test_cli.py::TestBase36RefValidation::test_real_hash_seed_ref_accepted` no longer depends on a randomly generated ID — the ID under test is fixed or deterministic.
- The test still exercises the HASH-shaped path: assert explicitly that the ID's suffix is non-numeric base36, and that assertion is now guaranteed rather than probabilistic.
- 40 consecutive full-suite runs are green: `for i in $(seq 40); do uv run pytest -q || break; done` completes without a failure.
- A grep for other tests asserting properties of freshly minted IDs (`isdigit`, ID-shape assertions after `jot`/`create`) turns up nothing else probabilistic, or any found are fixed the same way.
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
close_reason: test now pins HASH_ID='seeds-k3n7' via Database.create_seed instead of minting one and asserting it isn't all-digits; shape assertion kept as a guard on the literal. Second instance in test_hash_ids.py fixed (same seeds-skc category error). Full tests/ sweep found no other probabilistic ID assertion. 12-run soak green locally.

title: Add --add-tag / --remove-tag to seeds update (repeatable, silent no-op on absent)
description:
`seeds update --tags` replaces the whole tag set (`seed.tags = [...]`, src/seeds/cli.py:830). There are no additive operations. Changing one tag therefore requires reading all of them and retyping the rest — a read-modify-write whose write is never validated.

Source: seeds-aj6w.

## Motivation — this is correctness, not ergonomics

The only user of this CLI is an agent. Ryan: *"Remember, I don't actually ever use the CLI for seeds. It's all completely run by you."*

That is what makes it a correctness problem. A human retyping their own tags would notice one went missing. An agent reproducing a list from a `seeds show` it read two steps earlier will not, and nothing validates that the other tags survived. Silent loss, same shape as the `seeds update -c` footgun.

Measured on a real pending workflow: the `next-post` flag is live on **11 seeds** (queued blog posts). Clearing it today costs 11 `seeds show` calls plus 11 `--tags` writes **retyping 70 other tags**, each a silent-loss opportunity. Those tags are long and idiosyncratic — `meets-me-where-i-am`, `deliberation-is-the-artifact`, `destination-vs-journey`, `code-as-specification`. seeds-196 carries 10 tags; removing one means correctly reproducing nine of those.

Secondary benefit (relates to seeds-d773): read-modify-write burns an extra read per seed to change a few bytes. `--remove-tag next-post` needs none.

## Locked decisions — do NOT re-open

- **Keep `--tags` as-is.** It is the correct verb for setting tags at creation and for a deliberate full reset. This bead ADDS operations; it does not replace or deprecate anything. Tags split into topical ones (`workflow` 37x, `architecture` 34x — set once, never touched) and transient markers (`next-post` 11x, date tags — added to a batch then cleared). Only the second kind needs additive ops.
- **`--remove-tag` on a tag the seed does not carry is a SILENT NO-OP, not an error.** Ryan's call. Report the count of tags actually removed, so a typo like `--remove-tag next-posts` surfaces as "0 removed" rather than erroring mid-batch or vanishing without trace.
- **No batch form.** Ryan's call: *"looping is fine for now."* Do NOT add `--all-tagged` or any multi-seed selector. Revisit only if flags routinely span dozens of seeds.
- **No guard on tag operations.** Unlike `--content` (see the `update -c` bead), tags are working state and wholesale replacement is their normal verb. seeds-tk5y records that this asymmetry is deliberate — do not add symmetry for its own sake.

## Work

Add two repeatable options to `seeds update`:

- `--add-tag TEXT` (repeatable) — add a tag if not already present; adding an existing tag is also a no-op.
- `--remove-tag TEXT` (repeatable) — remove if present; silent no-op if absent.

Both must compose with each other in a single invocation. Interaction with `--tags` in the same command is an edge case worth deciding deliberately: simplest and most predictable is to reject combining `--tags` with either additive flag, since the intent is ambiguous. Make ONE pick and document it in the help text.

Preserve existing tag order where practical rather than re-sorting — tag order is currently authored, and gratuitous reordering would churn `.seeds/seeds.jsonl` diffs for every touched seed.
acceptance_criteria:
All against a temp SEEDS_DIR, never this project's real .seeds/:
- `seeds update <id> --add-tag foo` adds `foo` and leaves every pre-existing tag intact (verify the full set via `seeds show`).
- `--add-tag` is repeatable: `--add-tag a --add-tag b` adds both in one call.
- `--add-tag` with a tag the seed already has is a no-op and does not duplicate it.
- `seeds update <id> --remove-tag foo` removes only `foo`, leaving all others intact.
- `--remove-tag` on a tag the seed does NOT carry exits 0, changes nothing, and reports 0 removed (`seeds update <id> --remove-tag nope 2>&1 | grep -E '0'`).
- `--add-tag` and `--remove-tag` compose in one invocation.
- Wholesale `--tags` behavior is completely unchanged.
- Combining `--tags` with `--add-tag`/`--remove-tag` behaves as documented in the help text (whichever single behavior was chosen), and that behavior is covered by a test.
- Tag order of untouched tags is preserved (not re-sorted).
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
close_reason: --add-tag/--remove-tag added, repeatable, silent no-op on absent tags; preserves authored order; rejects --tags combined with additive flags and the same tag passed both ways; a no-op request skips the DB write so it cannot bump updated_at

title: Determine whether seeds import's last-write-wins upsert can silently overwrite newer deliberation
description:
Investigation, not a fix. Answer the question, record the finding, and only then decide whether follow-up work is warranted.

Source: seeds-tk5y (open question 2).

## The question

`seeds import` reconciles by `updated_at` with last-write-wins semantics (shipped in 0.3.3, seeds-155). Determine concretely: **can importing a stale JSONL discard deliberation that is newer than what the file carries?**

## Why this may matter more than the `-c` footgun it came from

`seeds update -c` requires a human or agent to type the wrong flag — there is an actor and a mistake. An import clobber would need neither. Plausible paths worth testing:

- A `git checkout` of an older commit, or a branch switch, leaves an older `.seeds/seeds.jsonl` on disk; the next `seeds sync` (which imports then exports) reconciles against it.
- Two machines working the same git-backed repo, one behind the other.
- A merge conflict resolved in favor of the older side.
- Clock skew making a stale record's `updated_at` look newer.

LWW is correct *given trustworthy timestamps*. The question is whether every path that reaches the import produces trustworthy ones.

## Work

1. Read the import path: `src/seeds/export.py` (`import_from_jsonl` and friends) and how `seeds sync` sequences import-then-export.
2. Determine empirically, in a temp `SEEDS_DIR` — never against this project's real `.seeds/`:
   - Create a seed, append to it (so `updated_at` advances), export.
   - Reconstruct an older JSONL for that seed (earlier `updated_at`, shorter body) and import it. Does the newer body survive?
   - Repeat with equal `updated_at` values and with a stale record whose timestamp is artificially newer.
3. Check whether `updated_at` is always server/local-clock generated at write time, or whether an imported record's own `updated_at` can be carried in verbatim and later re-exported as authoritative.
4. Record the finding — including "no exposure found," if that is the answer — in seeds-tk5y via `seeds update seeds-tk5y -a "..."`, and in this bead's notes.

## Deliverable

A clear yes/no with the reproduction, or a clear "not reachable, here is why." If the answer is yes, file a follow-up bead rather than fixing it here — the remedy (a guard? a backup? a merge strategy?) is a design decision, not a foregone one.

Do NOT change import behavior in this bead.
acceptance_criteria:
- The question is answered yes or no, with the evidence pasted into the bead notes.
- If YES: a minimal reproduction exists (exact commands against a temp SEEDS_DIR) showing newer deliberation being lost, AND a follow-up bead is filed describing the exposure.
- If NO: the bead notes state which specific mechanism prevents it (e.g. "updated_at is regenerated at write time, so an imported stale record cannot claim to be newer"), citing file:line.
- The finding is appended to seed seeds-tk5y.
- No behavior change is committed in this bead.
- This project's real `.seeds/` database is not mutated at any point.
notes:
## FINDING (investigation complete)

Answer to the question as literally posed — "can importing a stale JSONL discard
deliberation newer than what the file carries?" — is **NO**.
Answer to the concern behind it — "can a routine `seeds sync` silently destroy
newer deliberation?" — is **YES**, via the export half and via unverified
timestamps. Follow-up filed as **seeds-agk** (P1). No behaviour changed here.

All evidence below was produced in throwaway `SEEDS_DIR` labs under /tmp. The
project's real `.seeds/` was never mutated: `seeds.jsonl` md5 unchanged
(238a775c9678bb08ce76a67a7e90d83a before and after), `seeds.db` mtime unchanged.

### Q1. Older `updated_at` in the JSONL -> can it overwrite a newer DB body?

**No.** `export.py:235` is a strict `if seed.updated_at > existing.updated_at:`;
an older record falls through to `return "skipped"` at `export.py:244` and the DB
row is left alone. Reproduced: DB body "NEWER DELIBERATION: this append must
survive a stale import." with updated_at 18:08:51; imported a record for the same
ID rolled back to 18:08:50 with content "STALE". Result
`Imported: 0 created, 0 updated, 1 skipped`; DB body unchanged.

### Q2. Exactly EQUAL `updated_at`?

**DB wins.** The comparison is strictly `>`, so equal is not newer. Imported a
record with a byte-identical timestamp and content "EQUAL-TIMESTAMP CLOBBER
ATTEMPT": `0 created, 0 updated, 1 skipped`, DB body unchanged. This is what
makes re-import idempotent.

### Q3. Is the imported `updated_at` carried in verbatim and re-exported as authoritative?

**Yes, verbatim, by design.** `export.py:238` calls
`db.update_seed(seed, touch=False)`, and `db.py:451-452` (`if touch: seed.updated_at
= now_utc()`) only bumps the timestamp when `touch=True`. So the file's claimed
timestamp is written straight into the DB. Verified round-trip: imported a record
stamped +1h; `seeds sync --flush-only` re-exported `2026-08-10T19:08:51.480540+00:00`
byte-identical. The JSONL is therefore self-authenticating — nothing validates the
timestamp it claims.

### Q4. Does `seeds sync` create a path where stale on-disk state beats newer DB state?

**Yes — three of them.** `sync` is import (cli.py:1175) then unconditional export
(cli.py:1178), and `export_to_jsonl` opens the file `"w"` (export.py:100),
rewriting it wholesale from the DB with no comparison against what was on disk.

**(a) A merge resolution is silently reverted. No clock skew required.**
Repro (two machines, shared JSONL): B appends "B-SIDE DELIBERATION" at 18:10:46
and pushes. A appends "A-SIDE DELIBERATION" at 18:10:47 without pulling. A pulls;
the conflicted line is resolved **in favour of B**. A runs `seeds sync`:

    Imported: 0 created, 0 updated, 1 skipped
    Exported 1 seeds to .../seeds.jsonl

B's text is then gone from the file **and** absent from A's DB. The human's
explicit conflict resolution was reverted by the export half. The only signal is
"1 skipped" — identical to what every unchanged seed prints; a normal sync of this
repo would report `270 skipped`, so a real discard is invisible inside it.

**(b) Clock skew inverts the winner.** A +1h skew suffices. Repro: A typed the
genuinely-latest deliberation ("typed LAST, but on a slow clock") but B's record
carried a stamp 1h ahead. Import reported `0 created, 1 updated, 0 skipped` — a
healthy-looking sync — and A's newest body was wholesale-replaced by B's.

**(c) A future-dated record is permanently authoritative (self-sustaining).**
Once a record with `updated_at` ahead of local time is imported, every subsequent
*legitimate* local edit sets `updated_at = now_utc()` (db.py:452), which is
**earlier** than the stored future stamp — the seed's timestamp moves backward.
Repro with a +3650d stamp: after import the DB held 2036-08-07; a normal
`seeds update -a` then set it back to 2026-08-10; re-importing the same unchanged
file destroyed that local append (`0 created, 1 updated, 0 skipped`). The poisoned
record in git out-ranks every future local edit indefinitely.

**Also: LWW is a wholesale row replace, not a merge.** `db.update_seed` UPDATEs
title/content/status/tags/resolution as a unit (db.py:454-472). Since
`seeds update -a` (append) is the normal editing mode, two machines appending to
the same seed always lose one side entirely.

### Paths checked and ruled out

- **git checkout of an older commit + `seeds sync`: no seed loss.** Stale records
  are skipped, DB-only seeds are never deleted, and the export then rewrites the
  old commit's file from the full current DB. Repro: tree checked out with 1 seed,
  DB holding 3; after sync the tree held 3. Dirty working tree carrying later
  seeds on an old commit — pollution, not loss.
- **Relationship resurrection: not reachable.** Edges are re-asserted even for
  skipped records (export.py:243), but the CLI has no `delete`/`unlink` command,
  so there is nothing to resurrect.
- **v1 records cannot clobber at all** — `_import_v1_record` is create-only and
  returns "skipped" on an existing ID (export.py:116-117).
- **The real database is currently clean.** Read-only audit of all 270 records in
  `.seeds/seeds.jsonl`: 0 timezone-naive, 0 future-dated, 0 with
  `updated_at < created_at`. No poisoned record exists today.

### Separate robustness bug (noted, not fixed)

A timezone-naive `updated_at` raises an unhandled
`TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` at
export.py:235 and aborts the import mid-file. Records commit individually, so the
import is left partially applied. Loud rather than silent, so not data loss, but a
partial-write hazard. Captured in seeds-agk's description; may deserve its own bead.
close_reason: ANSWER: import alone is safe (older and equal both lose to the DB), but seeds sync can silently destroy newer deliberation via its unconditional export half and via verbatim-trusted file timestamps. Three paths confirmed; follow-up seeds-agk filed P1.

title: Guard seeds update -c: refuse to discard accumulated deliberation without --replace
description:
`seeds update -c/--content` replaces a seed's entire body with **no warning, no confirmation, no diff, no backup**. It sits one character away from `-a/--append`. For a tool whose purpose is preserving how thinking developed, that is a sharp edge pointed at the thing being protected.

Source: seeds-tk5y.

## Motivation

A seed whose deliberation is replaced is no longer a seed, it is a note. The value is reading how the thinking *moved*, including the parts that turned out wrong.

The failure mode is specifically an **agent** one: an agent reaching for `-c` when it meant `-a` destroys the record silently and reports success. Nothing in the output distinguishes the two outcomes.

`.seeds/seeds.jsonl` is git-tracked, so a clobbered body is recoverable via `git log -p` — but only if someone *knows it happened*. Nothing surfaces the loss at the time, so realistic discovery is noticing a seed reads oddly weeks later.

## Locked design — gate on whether deliberation exists, NOT on length

The legitimate uses of `-c` all share a shape: either nothing has accumulated yet, or it is an emergency that appending cannot solve. Both are detectable from fields the model already carries (`created_at`, `updated_at`; there is no revision count).

- **`updated_at == created_at`** (never been added to, so no deliberation exists) -> `-c` proceeds silently. This covers the common legitimate cases: a botched capture seconds old (shell quoting ate the content, a `$VAR` expanded, wrong paste buffer) and encoding repair.
- **Already updated** -> `-c` refuses. Print what would be discarded — character count plus the first line — and point at `-a` and at `--replace`.
- **`--replace`** -> explicit override. Exists for the one case appending genuinely cannot serve: redacting a credential or client name that must not exist in the body.

**Rejected — do not implement:** "warn when discarding more than N characters." Length is the wrong proxy. A 60-character seed refined over a week deserves more protection than a 4,000-character one pasted wrong ten seconds ago; a character threshold gets that exactly backwards. seeds-tk5y records this.

## Note on the redaction case

`--replace` stops the bleeding but does not finish the job: the old body remains in git history and needs separate scrubbing. Consider saying so in the `--replace` help text or in the refusal message, so nobody believes a secret is gone when it is not.

## Scope

- `--content` only. Leave `--title` alone. `--tags` also says "replaces existing" but carries little deliberation — out of scope here; seeds-tk5y notes the inconsistency should be deliberate rather than accidental.
- Do not touch `seeds import` — that is the sibling investigation bead.
acceptance_criteria:
- Fresh seed, never appended to: `seeds create -t "t" -c "original"` then `seeds update <id> -c "replaced"` SUCCEEDS silently, and `seeds show <id>` displays "replaced".
- Seed with accumulated deliberation: after `seeds update <id> -a "more"`, a subsequent `seeds update <id> -c "wiped"` exits NON-ZERO, leaves content unchanged (verify via `seeds show`), and its stderr names both `--append` and `--replace`.
- The refusal message includes the size of what would be discarded (character count) — `seeds update <id> -c "x" 2>&1 | grep -E '[0-9]+ char'` matches.
- `seeds update <id> -c "wiped" --replace` on that same seed SUCCEEDS and the content is replaced.
- `-a/--append` behavior is completely unchanged in all cases.
- `--title` remains replaceable with no guard.
- Tests cover: virgin-seed replace allowed, updated-seed replace refused, --replace override, append unaffected.
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
notes:
Implementation design picks (seeds-884/guard-content-replace):

1. Seed.updated_at now MIRRORS created_at at construction instead of taking a
   second now_utc() reading (models.py: UNSET_TIMESTAMP sentinel + __post_init__).
   Without this the locked "updated_at == created_at" gate never holds: the two
   default_factory calls drift, measured at ~8 microseconds on a fresh
   "seeds create", so every virgin seed would have read as already-edited.
   Consequence: seeds created BEFORE this change carry that drift and therefore
   read as edited, so -c on a legacy never-touched seed refuses and needs
   --replace. Conservative direction, and the refusal message explains the way
   out. A tolerance window (treat sub-millisecond gaps as unedited) was
   considered and rejected: it makes create -> append -> -c untestable without
   sleeping, since a test appends milliseconds after creating.

2. Empty (or whitespace-only) existing content -> -c proceeds even on an edited
   seed. "jot" then "explore" then "update -c <body>" is a normal flow, and there
   is nothing to discard; refusing would print "would discard 0 characters".
   The gate is whether deliberation exists, which an empty body settles.
close_reason: update -c now refuses on a seed that has been edited, naming --append and --replace and reporting the discarded size; required making Seed.updated_at mirror created_at at construction (two now_utc() reads drifted microseconds apart)

title: Validator rejects bead references: teach it to load bead IDs alongside seed IDs
description:
`_validate_id_refs` (src/seeds/cli.py:61) only knows about seed IDs. In this repo beads share the `seeds-` prefix with seeds, so **every legitimate bead reference inside a seed body reads as a hallucinated seed reference** and hard-fails seed creation.

Source: seeds-6hj5. This is the unambiguous-bug half of that concern; the judgment half is the sibling bead.

## Motivation

Recording bead lineage in a seed is *mandated* by the `seeds-to-beads` skill ("cite the originating seed IDs so the executor can recover deliberation context"). Today that mandated step fails, and the workaround is passing `--allow-unknown-refs` — which disables the hallucination check wholesale for that write. A required workflow step that requires disabling a safety feature is the smell.

Measured on the real 268-seed database: 24 distinct `seeds-*` tokens appear in seed text but are not seed IDs. **16 of them are real beads.** Fixing this removes two-thirds of the false alarms with no judgment calls.

## Work

Give the validator an optional second source of known IDs: the beads export at `.beads/issues.jsonl`.

- Locate it as a sibling of the seeds dir (seeds data lives in `.seeds/`, beads in `.beads/`, both at the project root). Resolve from the seeds dir's parent — do NOT hardcode a relative path from cwd.
- Parse it as JSONL, one object per line, taking the `id` field of each. Verified shape: `{"_type":"issue","id":"seeds-mlj",...}`. There are 94 IDs in it today.
- **This must be entirely optional.** seeds must keep working in a project with no beads at all: a missing `.beads/issues.jsonl` is the normal case, not an error. A malformed or unreadable one should also not break seed creation — degrade to "no bead IDs known" rather than crashing. Do NOT add beads as a dependency, and do NOT shell out to the `bd` CLI (it may not be installed; the JSONL is the git-tracked contract).
- A referenced ID that resolves to either a seed or a bead is valid; only tokens matching neither are candidates for "unknown".

## Explicitly out of scope

Do NOT try to fix hash-shaped-token validation here — today `find_id_refs` is called with no `known_ids`, so base36 tokens are dropped before they are ever checked. That is the sibling bead's job and it depends on this one. This bead's success condition is narrow: **bead references stop being rejected.**
acceptance_criteria:
- In this repo, `uv run seeds create -t "t" -c "see seeds-230"` (a real bead, all-digit suffix) succeeds WITHOUT `--allow-unknown-refs`. Clean up the created seed afterward, or run it against a temp SEEDS_DIR seeded to reproduce.
- A reference to a genuinely nonexistent all-digit ID (e.g. `seeds-99999`, matching neither a seed nor a bead) is STILL rejected — the check is not simply disabled.
- With no `.beads/` directory present at all (fresh temp SEEDS_DIR), `seeds create` and `seeds update` work normally and do not error or warn.
- With `.beads/issues.jsonl` present but corrupt (e.g. a single line of `not json`), `seeds create` still succeeds rather than crashing.
- A unit test covers all three states: beads file absent, present-and-valid, present-and-corrupt.
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
notes:
Implementation picks (seeds-90o):
1. Bead-ID loading lives in a new module src/seeds/beads.py (load_bead_ids / beads_issues_path) rather than inline in cli.py — keeps the optional, best-effort integration isolated and unit-testable without driving the CLI.
2. Read only .beads/issues.jsonl, not .beads/export/issues.jsonl. Both are git-tracked here, but export/ is stale (57 ids vs 99, missing seeds-230 and seeds-90o itself). The bead pinned the top-level file and it is the current one.
3. Partial corruption skips only the bad lines instead of discarding the whole file, so a truncated tail still contributes the ids it does have.
4. The export is read lazily — only when the text actually contains at least one candidate reference — so the common no-refs write does no I/O.
